title: Planets that loop backwards
teaches: Why planets sometimes run backwards across the sky, and why their orbits are ellipses

blocks.text: Watch the sky for a year and the stars behave themselves. They wheel round the pole each night and shift a little each season, but they keep their places relative to one another: the shape of Orion does not change. Five bright points refuse to cooperate. Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn drift through the constellations, which is why the Greeks called them *planetai*, wanderers.

Mostly they drift in one direction, eastward against the stars, slowly enough that you notice it over weeks. But every two years or so Mars does something peculiar. It slows, stops, and runs backwards, westward, for about ten weeks, then stops again and resumes its eastward course, having traced a loop or a zigzag on the sky. Jupiter and Saturn do the same thing, more often and in smaller loops. Any theory of the heavens had to explain this.

blocks.caption: Mars photographed night after night over several months, the frames combined into one picture: it runs east, stops, loops backwards and goes on.

blocks.text: Claudius Ptolemy, working in Alexandria around 150 AD, explained it with circles riding on circles. Each planet moved on a small circle, the **epicycle**, whose centre moved on a big circle round the Earth. Most of the time the two motions added up and the planet crept forward; but on the inner part of the small circle it moved the opposite way to the big one, fast enough to win, and it appeared to go backwards. With enough adjustments the scheme predicted[^equant] planetary positions well enough to be used for fourteen hundred years.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Planets drift eastward against the stars, but each one regularly stops, runs westward for a while and turns east again: [[retrograde motion]].
Ptolemy explained it with small circles riding on large ones, centred on the Earth.

blocks.text: In 1543 Nicolaus Copernicus, a canon of Frombork Cathedral in Poland, published a book arguing that the Sun, not the Earth, sits at the centre, with the Earth as one more planet going round it. He had worked on it for thirty years and saw the first printed copy, the story goes, on the day he died. One of its strongest points was what it did to the backward loops.

blocks.caption: Copernicus's own diagram of the Sun-centred system, from *De revolutionibus* (1543).

blocks.text: If the Earth is a planet, and inner planets go round faster than outer ones, then every so often the Earth overtakes Mars, the way a runner on the inside lane of a track laps a slower runner on the outside. While the inside runner is passing, the slower one seems to slide backwards against the distant stands, even though both are running forwards the whole time. Mars against the stars is the outside runner against the stands.

blocks.caption: The Earth and an outer planet on their orbits (left), and the planet's track against the distant stars as seen from Earth (right). The yellow line is our line of sight.
blocks.task: Make a prediction, then move through the days until you see the planet run backwards

blocks.text: This explains several things for free. For an outer planet, the loop always happens when it is opposite the Sun in our sky, high at midnight, because that is when the Earth lies between it and the Sun: the moment we draw level on the inside track and pass it. Farther planets loop more often, because they move so slowly that we lap them sooner, and through a smaller angle, because the same sideways swerve of the Earth makes a smaller shift in something farther away (hold up a finger and look at it with each eye in turn, then try with your arm outstretched; *How far are the stars?* makes much of this). Ptolemy had to arrange these facts by hand; for Copernicus they fell out of the geometry.

But Copernicus still believed, like most astronomers since Plato, that heavenly motion had to be made of uniform circles. When simple Sun-centred circles didn't quite match the sky, he too had to add small epicycles. His system was simpler in spirit but no more accurate than Ptolemy's. Something was still wrong.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: With the Sun at the centre, retrograde loops come from the faster inner planet overtaking the slower outer one.
Outer planets loop when opposite the Sun in our sky; farther planets make smaller loops.

blocks.text: The trouble was data. **Tycho Brahe**, a Danish nobleman with a temper, a fortune and a metal nose (he had lost part of the original in a duel over a mathematical point), built the finest observatory of the age on the island of Hven. His instruments had no lenses; the telescope did not yet exist. What they had was size and care: a brass arc about two metres in radius fixed to a wall, sights read by assistants, every measurement checked. For twenty years Tycho logged planetary positions to a routine accuracy of a minute or two of arc, roughly five times better than anyone before him.

blocks.caption: Tycho's great wall quadrant at Uraniborg, from his 1598 book. Tycho himself is painted on the wall, pointing at the sky.

blocks.text: In 1600 he hired a brilliant, impecunious German mathematician, **[[Johannes Kepler]]**, and soon set him on the hardest problem in the collection: the orbit of Mars. Tycho died the next year, and Kepler, after some unpleasantness with the heirs, kept the observations.[^witch]

Kepler spent nearly five years on what he called his war with Mars. He tried one circular scheme after another, shifting the centre and adjusting speeds. In the traditional telling, one model fitted Tycho's observations at opposition to within two minutes of arc, but at other points it missed by eight minutes, about a quarter of the width of the full Moon.[^eight-minutes] Earlier astronomers would have shrugged; their own observations were no better than that. Kepler trusted Tycho. "These eight minutes alone," he wrote, "have pointed the way to a reformation of all astronomy." He gave up the circle.

blocks.caption: Kepler's circle for Mars, with the Sun off centre and the planet sweeping equal areas in equal times, against Mars as it really moves, seen from the Sun. The green band is Tycho's accuracy.
blocks.task: Squeeze the circle until the model stays inside Tycho's accuracy all year

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Tycho Brahe measured planet positions to about one or two minutes of arc, without a telescope.
Kepler's circular model for Mars missed Tycho's data by eight minutes of arc, and he believed the data rather than the circle.

blocks.text: What finally fitted, in 1605, was an **[[ellipse]]**, a stretched circle, with the Sun not at the centre but off to one side at a point called a **focus**. Kepler published this in 1609 in *Astronomia nova*, the New Astronomy, along with a rule about speed that he had found first, around 1602, and that is now called his second law. A planet goes faster when it is near the Sun and slower when it is far. Precisely: the line from the Sun to the planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times.

blocks.caption: An orbit with the Sun at one focus. The dots mark where the planet is at each twelfth of its year, and each coloured wedge is swept out in the same time.
blocks.task: Make a prediction, then stretch the orbit and watch where the planet moves fastest

blocks.text: Mars's orbit is round to within half a per cent, so if you drew it you would hardly see that it isn't a circle; what shows is that the Sun sits about 9 per cent of the radius off centre (an **eccentricity** of 0.093). That was why it took so long to find. The flattening is small enough to hide in poor data and just large enough to stand out in Tycho's.

Ten years later Kepler added a third rule. The farther a planet is from the Sun, the longer its year, in a fixed proportion: the square of the time to go round is in proportion to the cube of the orbit's average distance from the Sun. Saturn, about nine and a half times as far as the Earth, takes about twenty-nine and a half years. Kepler found these three rules, but he did not know why planets obeyed them; Newton did, in the next lesson.

blocks.caption: From Ptolemy's circles to Kepler's ellipses.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Kepler's first rule: planets move on ellipses with the Sun at one focus.
Second rule: the line from the Sun to a planet sweeps equal areas in equal times, so planets move fastest near the Sun.
Third rule: farther planets take longer to go round, the square of the period in proportion to the cube of the average distance.

blocks.caption: Six questions on loops and ellipses
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: Mars traced this loop against the stars. What was really happening?
choices: The Earth was overtaking Mars on its smaller, faster orbit
Mars was stopping and reversing along its own orbit
Mars was riding round a small epicycle of its own
items.why: Mars keeps moving forward on its orbit. As we pass it, our line of sight to it swings backwards against the far stars.

items.ask: When in our sky does Mars run backwards?
choices: When it is opposite the Sun, high at midnight
When it is close to the Sun, low in the west at dusk
items.why: We overtake Mars when the Earth lies between it and the Sun, which puts Mars opposite the Sun in our sky.

items.ask: Why does Jupiter's backward loop span a smaller angle than Mars's?
choices: Jupiter is farther away, so the Earth's shift makes a smaller angle
Jupiter moves faster on its orbit, so we pass it more quickly
items.why: The loop comes from the Earth's own motion seen against the far planet. The farther the planet, the smaller the angle that motion makes.

items.ask: Why did Kepler abandon circular orbits?
choices: His best circle missed Tycho's Mars data by eight minutes of arc
Copernicus had already shown that planetary orbits are ellipses
Circular orbits could not produce the backward loops at all
items.why: Tycho's data were good to a minute or two of arc, so a misfit of eight minutes was real. Kepler trusted the data over the circle.

items.ask: A comet's orbit is a long, thin ellipse. Where does it move fastest?
choices: Where it swings closest to the Sun
Out at the far end of its orbit, away from the Sun
It keeps the same steady speed all the way round
items.why: Equal areas in equal times: near the Sun the line to the comet is short, so it has to sweep fast to cover the same area.

items.ask: What instruments gave Tycho his precise measurements?
choices: West, because it is in the middle of its backward loop
East, as it does on every night of the year
items.why: Tycho worked before the telescope. His accuracy came from the size and care of instruments like the two-metre quadrant.

summary: **Retrograde loops come from overtaking.** A faster inner planet passes a slower outer one, so an outer planet seen from the Earth runs backwards when it is opposite the Sun.
**Orbits are ellipses, the Sun at one focus.** Kepler found it because he would not ignore an eight-minute miss in Tycho Brahe’s naked-eye positions.
**Planets move fastest nearest the Sun.** The line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times.
**Farther planets take longer to go round.** The square of the period is in proportion to the cube of the average distance.

equant.title: The equant
equant.text: Ptolemy's most important adjustment was the **equant**, a point off the centre of the big circle about which the epicycle's centre turned at a steady rate. It let a planet speed up and slow down, as real planets do, while every circle still turned evenly about something. Copernicus thought it a cheat and replaced it with extra small circles.

witch.title: Kepler's mother
witch.text: Kepler's life was not quiet. In 1615 his mother, Katharina, was accused of witchcraft in Württemberg, and he spent years conducting her defence himself. She was held in chains for more than a year and shown the instruments of torture before she was released in 1621; she died six months later.

eight-minutes.title: The eight minutes
eight-minutes.text: The eight-minute discrepancy in sky position (longitude) was real, and Kepler made it the rhetorical centrepiece of *Astronomia nova*. In practice he was just as troubled by Mars's varying distance from the Sun, which he triangulated using Earth's own orbit and which his circular model also got wrong.
